catalog_quote: [Gómez Rendón 2013: 33] A propósito Jijón y Caamaño notó oportunamente que además del acento prosódico en la penúltima sílaba que poseen la mayoría de palabras del esmeraldeño, existiría otro que él llama “acento musical” (1940-II: 427), a juzgar por los grafemas con que Pallares representó la terminación {àãle} en palabras como sakàãle ‘ahogado’ o yatàãle ‘acabado’, donde la primera /a/ pertenece más bien a la raíz verbal. ... La presencia de tono, el segundo rasgo vocálico característico del esmeraldeño, permitiría explicar incluso el hecho de que muchas veces se tilden palabras graves, cuando lo normal es no hacerlo, y que se lo haga aparentemente con un sentido contrastivo (Jijón y Caamaño, 1940-II: 426). || [Adelaar & Muysken 2004: 156, Google Books snippet] ... past participle (e.g. in yatáále 'finished'). The accent is often indicated with a diacritic (by Seler in particular), suggesting that stress was contrastive.
world_status: statement found in an open source

The accent is often indicated with a diacritic (by Seler in particular), suggesting that stress was contrastive. The consonant inventory comprised voiceless and voiced stops (p, t, k; b, d, g)... || [Gómez Rendón 2013: 33] A propósito Jijón y Caamaño notó oportunamente que además del acento prosódico en la penúltima sílaba que poseen la mayoría de palabras del esmeraldeño, existiría otro que él llama “acento musical” (1940-II: 427) ... permitiría explicar incluso el hecho de que muchas veces se tilden palabras graves, cuando lo normal es no hacerlo, y que se lo haga aparentemente con un sentido contrastivo (Jijón y Caamaño, 1940-II: 426).
new_statements.translation: Gómez Rendón: 'In this connection Jijón y Caamaño aptly noted that, besides the prosodic accent on the penultimate syllable that most Esmeraldeño words have, there would be another that he calls "musical accent" (1940-II: 427) ... [tone] would even explain the fact that paroxytone words are often written with an accent mark, when the norm is not to do so, and that this is apparently done with a contrastive sense (Jijón y Caamaño 1940-II: 426).'

new_statements.locator: Adelaar & Muysken 2004: §2.19, p. 156 (Google Books pg=PA156); Gómez Rendón 2013: p. 33
new_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Both quoted passages are present in the copies we hold at (1) Adelaar & Muysken 2004: 156 -- the dc:description of Google Books volumes feed, book id UiwaUY6KsY8C, pg=PA156) reads '.. past participle ( e.g. in yatáále ' finished '). The ac- cent is often indicated with a diacritic ( by Seler in particular), suggesting that stress was contrastive. The consonant inventory comprised voiceless and voiced stops ( p..', and overlaps and continues '( p, t, k; b, d, g); a voiceless affricate ( ch)..'. Only differences from the report's quote: the snippet has 'yatáále' (report typed 'yatáale') and line-break hyphenation 'ac- cent'. (2) Gómez Rendón 2013 -- lines 1816-1827, which fall directly under…
new_statements.rule_in_words: All that can be said rests on the accent marks in Pallares' 1877 Spanish-orthography wordlist: most words appear to be stressed on the penult (Jijón y Caamaño via Gómez Rendón), but the diacritics fall often enough and unpredictably enough that Adelaar infers stress was contrastive (lexical); no rule is recoverable and the language is extinct.
new_statements.exceptions: Jijón y Caamaño's 'acento musical' on the past-participle ending written -àà/-áá/-àã (e.g. yatáale 'finished', sakàãle 'drowned'), which Adelaar reports as a special vowel sound and Gómez Rendón reinterprets as tone.
new_statements.domain_note: Philological inference from written accents on isolated words and short phrases in a single 19th-century wordlist; no phonetic observation of speech; word-level only.
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe the same and only attestation: the vocabulary collected by J. M. Pallares at Esmeraldas in 1877 for Teodoro Wolf and published by Seler (1902); 'Atacame' (Glottolog name) = 'Esmeraldeño' of Adelaar, Jijón y Caamaño and Gómez Rendón (atac1235). No dialect differentiation is possible.

tone_statements.citation: Gómez Rendón, Jorge Arsenio. 2013. El esmeraldeño: ¿una lengua prehispánica en el siglo XIX? Informe de investigación PI-2013-05 (serie Proyectos de Investigación UASB, Sede Ecuador). Quito: Universidad Andina Simón Bolívar, Sede Ecuador. 104 pp.
tone_statements.quote: ... nos parece más que plausible que el acento musical que menciona Jijón y Caamaño sea un rasgo suprasegmental que se conoce en lingüística como tono. La presencia de tono, el segundo rasgo vocálico característico del esmeraldeño, permitiría explicar incluso el hecho de que muchas veces se tilden palabras graves, cuando lo normal es no hacerlo, y que se lo haga aparentemente con un sentido contrastivo (Jijón y Caamaño 1940, II: 426). Cuando vamos en busca de lenguas con sistemas tonales, aunque sean simples como en el caso del esmeraldeño (un solo tono distintivo), encontramos un problema.
tone_statements.translation: ... it seems to us more than plausible that the musical accent Jijón y Caamaño mentions is the suprasegmental feature known in linguistics as tone. The presence of tone, the second characteristic vocalic feature of Esmeraldeño, would even explain why paroxytone words are often given an accent mark when the norm is not to, apparently with a contrastive sense (Jijón y Caamaño 1940, II: 426). When we look for languages with tonal systems, even simple ones as in the case of Esmeraldeño (a single distinctive tone), we meet a problem.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 65-66, section 3 'Análisis de la evidencia lingüística.. / La lengua esmeraldeña en el corpus Pallares-Wolf', paragraph on the vowel system
tone_statements.summary: Author posits penultimate prosodic accent for most words plus lexical/grammatical tone ('un solo tono distintivo', i.e. one marked tone), evidenced by the participle ending -àãle and by contrastively accented paroxytones; origin attributed to an African (Bantu) contact language; no TBU, inventory or rules beyond that; entirely inferential from 1877 orthography.

tone_statements.citation: Jijón y Caamaño, Jacinto. 1941. El Ecuador interandino y occidental antes de la conquista castellana, tomo II (chapter 'El Esmeraldeño', c. pp. 424-540; accent on pp. 426-427). Quito: Editorial Ecuatoriana; reprinted Quito: Abya-Yala 1998.
tone_statements.quote: Además del acento prosódico o dinámico, de que hemos venido hablando, hay en Esmeraldeño huellas de un acento musical en la terminación ààle del participio, que Pallares interpretó advirtiendo «las dos a a con larga aspiración» (1). Seler creyó que se trataba de una aa larga, mas como se ve por los ejemplos siguientes: sakààle=ahogado, yatààle=acabado, la primera a pertenece al sufijo precedente, por lo cual parécenos más probable el que se trate de un acento musical que afecta a ambas a.
tone_statements.translation: Besides the prosodic or dynamic accent we have been discussing, there are in Esmeraldeño traces of a musical accent in the participle ending ààle, which Pallares interpreted by noting 'the two a a with long aspiration' (1). Seler believed it was a long aa, but as the following examples show: sakààle 'drowned', yatààle 'finished', the first a belongs to the preceding suffix, so it seems to us more probable that it is a musical accent affecting both a's.
tone_statements.locator: pp. 426-427, cap. XXV 'El idioma esmeraldeño', sec. II Fonética; fn. (1) = Seler, op. cit. p. 61
tone_statements.summary: Philological reading of Pallares/Seler records of a dead language: dynamic accent mostly penultimate (some antepenult, final) plus hedged 'traces' of a musical accent only on participial -aale.

sources.note: p.33 (typological profile of Esmeraldeño from the Pallares-Wolf corpus, following Jijón y Caamaño 1941 II: 425-480 and Adelaar 2004): most Esmeraldeño words carry prosodic accent on the penultimate syllable (after Jijón y Caamaño 1941 II: 427); Pallares' written accents on paroxytone words appear to be used contrastively (J&C II: 426); J&C's additional 'acento musical' on the participle ending -àãle is reinterpreted by Gómez Rendón as tone.
Paraphrases Adelaar 2004: 'El acento se indica frecuentemente en las fuentes, y parece que la posición del acento pudo haber sido fonológicamente distintiva.' Second-hand only.
